title: Absolute Temperature and the Kelvin Scale
short_intro: Absolute temperature is a thermodynamic measure of temperature scaled from absolute zero, the theoretical state where particles possess minimum thermal motion and zero entropy. It is fundamentally defined via the second law of thermodynamics using Carnot engines, making it independent of the working substance.

exam_scope.tgt_core: Definition of absolute zero, conversion between Celsius, Fahrenheit, and Kelvin temperature scales, triple point of water, and basic gas law relationships based on absolute temperature.
exam_scope.pgt_extension: Thermodynamic temperature scale definition via Carnot efficiency, Kelvin's work function, limitations at absolute zero (Third Law of Thermodynamics), and kinetic theory interpretation of absolute temperature.

prerequisites: Zeroth and First Laws of Thermodynamics
Ideal Gas Equation and Kinetic Theory of Gases

concept_notes.heading: Definition and Thermodynamic Basis
bullets: Absolute temperature is measured on the Kelvin scale, where 0 K represents absolute zero.
It is independent of the thermometric properties of any particular substance, unlike mercury-in-glass or constant-volume gas thermometers.
The thermodynamic temperature scale is established using the efficiencies of reversible Carnot engines operating between two heat reservoirs.

concept_notes.heading: Ideal Gas Scale vs Thermodynamic Scale
bullets: In the limit of zero pressure, an ideal gas thermometer defines an absolute temperature scale that is identical to the thermodynamic Kelvin scale.
The pressure of a given mass of gas at constant volume extrapolates to zero at absolute zero temperature (-273.15 deg C).
Real gases deviate from this ideal behavior at high pressures and low temperatures due to intermolecular forces.

concept_notes.heading: Triple Point of Water Reference
bullets: Since 1954 and reaffirmed in the 2019 SI redefinition, the Kelvin is defined by fixing the Boltzmann constant k to exactly 1.380649 x 10<sup>-23</sup> J K<sup>-1</sup>.
Historically and practically, it is anchored to the triple point of water, where ice, liquid water, and water vapor coexist in equilibrium.
The temperature of the triple point of water is defined as exactly 273.16 K.

concept_notes.heading: Kinetic Interpretation
bullets: According to the kinetic theory of gases, the absolute temperature of an ideal gas is directly proportional to the average translational kinetic energy per molecule.
Equipartition of energy states that each active degree of freedom contributes (1/2)k<sub>B</sub>T to the internal energy per molecule.
At absolute zero, molecular motion ceases entirely, though quantum zero-point energy remains in harmonic oscillators.

derivations.title: Thermodynamic Temperature Scale from Carnot Efficiency
derivations.conditions: Reversible Carnot engine operating between temperatures T_1 and T_2
steps: The efficiency eta of any reversible engine operating between two heat reservoirs at empirical temperatures theta_1 and theta_2 depends only on these temperatures: eta = 1 - Q_2/Q_1 = f(theta_1, theta_2).

Consider three engines operating with heat exchanges Q_1, Q_2, and Q_3 at temperatures theta_1, theta_2, and theta_3 such that Q_2/Q_1 = f(theta_1, theta_2), Q_3/Q_2 = f(theta_2, theta_3), and Q_3/Q_1 = f(theta_1, theta_3).
Since Q_3/Q_1 = (Q_3/Q_2) x (Q_2/Q_1), it follows that f(theta_1, theta_3) = f(theta_1, theta_2) x f(theta_2, theta_3).
This functional equation implies that the ratio of heats can be written as the ratio of a universal function of temperature alone: Q_2/Q_1 = T_2/T_1.
Defining T as this absolute temperature scale gives eta = 1 - T_2/T_1.

derivations.title: Relation between Absolute Temperature and Mean Kinetic Energy
steps: The pressure of an ideal gas from kinetic theory is given by P = (1/3)(Nm/V)v_{rms}^2.
Using the ideal gas law PV = N k_B T, equate the two expressions: (1/3)Nm v_{rms}^2 = N k_B T.
Rearrange to solve for the total translational kinetic energy E_k = (3/2)N k_B T.
Divide by N to find the average translational kinetic energy per molecule: <E_k> = (3/2)k_B T.

graphs_and_experiments.title: Pressure vs Celsius Temperature for Real and Ideal Gases
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: A set of straight lines for different gases on a P vs t (°C) plot, all converging to a single intercept on the temperature axis at -273.15 °C when extrapolated.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: Demonstrates that pressure vanishes at absolute zero for all dilute gases, establishing the universal absolute zero reference point.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Frequently tested in TGT/PGT to check understanding of temperature axis intercept extrapolation in gas thermometry.

solved_numericals.question: At what temperature is the Fahrenheit scale reading equal to twice the Celsius scale reading?
solution_steps: Let the Celsius temperature be t. Then the Fahrenheit temperature is F = 2t.
Substitute F = 2t into the equation: (2t - 32)/9 = t/5.
Verify Fahrenheit reading: F = 2(160) = 320°F. Check: (320 - 32)/9 = 288/9 = 32, and 160/5 = 32. Both match.

solved_numericals.question: Calculate the root mean square velocity of oxygen molecules (M = 32 g/mol) at an absolute temperature of 300 K. Given R = 8.314 J mol^-1 K^-1.
solution_steps: Identify given parameters: T = 300 K, M = 32 g/mol = 32 x 10^-3 kg/mol, R = 8.314 J mol^-1 K^-1.
Write the formula for root mean square velocity: v_{rms} = sqrt(3RT / M).
Substitute values: v_{rms} = sqrt((3 x 8.314 x 300) / (32 x 10^-3)).
Take square root: sqrt(233831.25) approx 483.56 m/s.

solved_numericals.question: A Carnot engine absorbs 1200 kJ of heat from a reservoir at 500 K and rejects heat to a sink at 300 K. Calculate the work done by the engine and the entropy change of the universe during one cycle.
solution_steps: Identify given values: Q_H = 1200 kJ, T_H = 500 K, T_C = 300 K.
Find efficiency of the Carnot engine: eta = 1 - (T_C / T_H) = 1 - (300/500) = 1 - 0.6 = 0.4.
Calculate work done: W = eta x Q_H = 0.4 x 1200 kJ = 480 kJ.
Calculate heat rejected to sink: Q_C = Q_H - W = 1200 - 480 = 720 kJ.
Calculate entropy change of source: Delta S_H = -Q_H / T_H = -1200 kJ / 500 K = -2.4 kJ/K.
Calculate entropy change of sink: Delta S_C = Q_C / T_C = 720 kJ / 300 K = +2.4 kJ/K.
Total entropy change of the universe for a reversible cycle: Delta S_univ = Delta S_H + Delta S_C = -2.4 + 2.4 = 0.
solved_numericals.answer: Work done = 480 kJ, Universe entropy change = 0

assumptions_and_limitations: Absolute zero (0 K) is unattainable in finite operational steps, as stated by the Third Law of Thermodynamics.
Real gases liquefy or solidify before reaching absolute zero, making the ideal gas scale extrapolation hypothetical at extreme lows.

common_misconceptions.wrong: Absolute zero means molecules stop moving completely and have zero total energy.
common_misconceptions.correct: Molecules possess minimum energy corresponding to quantum zero-point energy, but translational kinetic energy vanishes macroscopically.
common_misconceptions.why: Heisenberg's Uncertainty Principle prevents particles from having simultaneously zero position uncertainty and zero momentum.

common_misconceptions.wrong: The Kelvin scale depends on the properties of the thermometric substance used.
common_misconceptions.correct: The thermodynamic Kelvin scale is completely independent of any working substance.
common_misconceptions.why: It is defined via Carnot engine efficiencies operating between heat reservoirs.

quick_revision: Absolute zero is 0 K or -273.15 °C, where ideal gas pressure and molecular translational kinetic energy extrapolate to zero.
Celsius to Kelvin Conversion: T = t + 273.15
